title: Revelation is unwritten or written; one Word in substance, dual in mode; against a real pontifical distinction
pass_a_gloss: XXII. Secondly, divine revelation is non-scripta or scripta. Things divine are not able to be known except through God and the word of him, whether this be the agraphon (non-scriptum) or the eggraphon (scriptum). Whatever truly is known out of it, that returns unto this principle: Whatever God said, is to be believed; or the mouth of the Lord has spoken, Therefore it is to be believed. This Word, how much unto the substance of doctrine, is entirely one; but by the mode of revelation as it were double, non-scriptum and scriptum it is called. Here however the mode of revelation is chiefly to be unfolded. For although all things revealed from one and the same Spirit proceed, not nevertheless all by the same mode are laid open. For certain things are written; certain are collected, as teach Gregory Nazianzen book 5 On Theology, Basil the Great On true faith, Augustine On Baptism against the Donatists book 2 chapter 14 and book 4 chapter 23. Certain things are not, and yet are said to be in the scriptures, as God to sit, to have ears, eyes. Certain things are, nor yet expressly and in just so many words are said, as the Holy Spirit to be God; something nevertheless is said, whence that necessarily is concluded, as who twice five says, ten says; and who twice two, four says, although not in just so many words. Certain things truly neither are, nor are said. Certain finally both are and are said. Who truly a real distinction with the pontiffs establish between the word of God written and non-written, those gravely err. For wisely Irenaeus book 3 against heresies chapter 1: Not through others the disposition of our salvation have we known, than through those through whom the Gospel arrived unto us, which indeed then they heralded, afterwards truly through the will of God in the scriptures unto us they handed down as foundation and pillar of our faith to be.
pass_b_english: XXII. Second: divine revelation is either unwritten or written. Divine things can be known only through God and his word — whether that word is ἄγραφον, unwritten, or ἔγγραφον, written. Whatever is known from it returns to this principle: Whatever God has said must be believed; or, The mouth of the Lord has spoken, therefore it must be believed.

As to the substance of doctrine this Word is altogether one; as to the mode of revelation it is, as it were, twofold — unwritten and written. That mode of revelation is what chiefly needs explanation. Although everything revealed proceeds from one and the same Spirit, not everything is disclosed in the same way. Some things are written; some are gathered by inference — as Gregory Nazianzen teaches in book 5 On Theology, Basil the Great in On the true faith, and Augustine in On Baptism against the Donatists, book 2 chapter 14 and book 4 chapter 23.

Some things are not, and yet are said to be in the Scriptures — that God sits, that he has ears and eyes. Some things are, and yet are not said expressly and in so many words — that the Holy Spirit is God — though something is said from which the point follows of necessity, as when one who says twice five says ten, and one who says twice two says four, even without using those exact words. Some things neither are nor are said. Finally, some both are and are said.

Those who join the papists in setting a real distinction between the written and the unwritten word of God go badly astray. Irenaeus speaks wisely (Against heresies, book 3, chapter 1): We have known the disposition of our salvation through no others than those through whom the Gospel reached us — which they first heralded, and afterwards, by God's will, handed down to us in the Scriptures as the foundation and pillar of our faith to come.
source_text:
XXII. 2. Divina revelatio est non scripta aut scripta.
Res divinae non possunt nisi per Deum, ejusque verbum cognosci, sive hoc sit ἄγραφον non-scriptum, sive ἔγγραφον scriptum. Quicquid vero ex eo cognoscitur, id redit ad hoc principium: Quicquid Deus dixit, credendum est: vel os Domini locutum est, Ergo credendum est. Verbum hoc, quantum ad substantiam doctrinae, prorsus unum est, sed modo revelationis quasi duplex, non-scriptum & scriptum dicitur. Hic autem revelationis modus praecipue explicandus est. Quamvis enim omnia revelata ab uno eodemque proficiscuntur spiritu, non tamen omnia eodem modo patefiunt. Quaedam enim scribuntur; quaedam colliguntur, ut docent Gregorius Nazianzenus lib. 5. de Theol. Basilius Magnus de vera fide, Augustinus de Bapt. contra Donatistas lib. 2. cap. 14. & lib. 4. cap. 23. Quaedam non sunt, & tamen dicuntur esse in scripturis, ut Deum sedere, habere aures, oculos. Quaedam sunt, nec tamen expresse & totidem verbis dicuntur, ut Spiritum sanctum esse Deum, aliquid tamen dicitur, unde id necessario concludatur, ut qui bis quinque dicit, decem dicit: & qui bis duo, quatuor dicit, licet non totidem verbis. Quaedam vero neque sunt, neque dicuntur. Quaedam denique & sunt & dicuntur. Qui vero reale discrimen cum pontificiis statuunt inter verbum Dei scriptum & non-scriptum, ii graviter errant. Scite enim Irenaeus lib. 3. adversus haer. cap. 1. Non per alios dispositionem salutis nostrae cognovimus, quam per eos, per quos Euangelium pervenit ad nos, quod quidem tunc praeconiaverunt, postea vero per Dei voluntatem in scripturis nobis tradiderunt fundamentum & columnam fidei nostrae futurum.
